title: Even Birds Get Jet Lag
summary: New research says humans are not the only ones who get jet lag. Some birds may get it too. A study in Science looked at Manx shearwaters, a common bird in the British Isles. They look a little like seagulls but are closely related to albatrosses, said Patrick Lewin of the University of Oxford. Shearwater pairs mate for life and lay just one egg. They take turns sitting on it: one partner stays on the egg while the other goes to sea. The hunting partner may spend up to two weeks hunting fish and squid in the North Atlantic, often hundreds of miles from home. Then it races back to its colony, often in a day or so. The birds are believed to use the sun to find their way. That only works if they know the time of day. But when they rush home, their inner clocks fall out of sync with the sun, so they veer slightly off course. At most, a seven-degree error took a bird about three miles out of its way on a 600-mile trip.
why_it_matters: It shows that even animals can feel mixed up when their body clocks do not match the world around them, just like you might after a long trip or a late night.

Some birds seem to use the sun to guide them, and that only works if their inner sense of time matches the real time of day.
